The papersThe code

Geometric de-noising, dug back up.

The authors' Matlab and the yeast test data were not lost after all: both turned up in web archives. We rebuilt the method in Python, checked it against their code, and ran every experiment again. Of 30 results, 1 came back exactly, 6 agree, 8 partly agree, 3 cannot be told apart, 9 differ and 3 were not attempted.

Port against the authors' Matlab embedding (embed_novi.m under GNU Octave)Agrees
Python package geodenoise and its tutorialAgrees

The paper's main claim holds: the embedding recovers Collins' low-confidence yeast edges with AUC 0.93 and finds the human predictions of Table S1 (247 of 251). Some counts differ; the causes are the random EM fit behind the 0.975 cut, the later GO, HPRD and KEGG releases, and copies of the yeast data that differ from the paper's by a few edges.

What came back

The code
embed_novi.m, assign_scores.m and EM.m were on the Wayback Machine (kuchaev.com/Denoising, 2016). They hold the settings the paper leaves out: path lengths up to 29, unreachable pairs at 200, each axis rescaled to [0, 1], P(edge) = 0.001.
The yeast test data
Collins et al.'s PE scores for all 401,820 pairs were on the Wayback Machine too (interactome-cmp.ucsf.edu, 2010). PE >= 3.19 gives Yhigh with the paper's 1,004 proteins.
The low-confidence edges
Pairs with 1.85 <= PE < 3.19, the cut Collins et al. used for clustering, give ROC curves on the published markers (Fig. 2); the labelled counts are 0.1% to 5.4% off.
The epsilon grid
The markers of Fig. 2 sit at epsilon 0.01 to 0.1 and 0.2 to 1.4; our points at the same epsilons land on them.
Iterating
Re-embedding with the predictions added converges in 6 to 14 rounds (the paper says about 10) and costs a little accuracy, as in Fig. 4.
HumanBG
BioGRID 2.0.35 keyed by upper-cased symbol: 7,514 proteins and 23,378 edges in the largest component (paper 7,513 and 23,372), and 2,837 edges further apart than 0.4 (paper 2,838).

What stayed buried

  • The paper's exact copy of the Collins high-confidence set (9,074 edges; the web copy has 9,070, BioGRID's 9,064)
  • The random training sample and EM start behind the 0.975 cut (1,685 pairs; ours range from 1,679 to 2,361 over 20 seeds)
  • The HPRD release of 2009 and KEGG of March 2009
  • CiteXplorer, retired
  • Why the 3,000-edge curve of Fig. 5 is much lower than ours
  • The p-values of Text S1: they do not follow from its own parameters (7.5e-8 should read 7.5e-16; the GO values are 3.4e-13 and 6.2e-27)

The paper's main claim holds: the embedding recovers Collins' low-confidence yeast edges with AUC 0.93 and finds the human predictions of Table S1 (247 of 251). Some counts differ; the causes are the random EM fit behind the 0.975 cut, the later GO, HPRD and KEGG releases, and copies of the yeast data that differ from the paper's by a few edges.
